In 2017, Norway divided its coast into production zones and began adjusting each zone's allowed growth according to measured lice levels on nearby wild salmon. Researchers studying the system note that the damage from a pen depends heavily on its location: a farm near a major salmon river's migration route can do far more harm than an equally large farm in a fjord that wild fish rarely pass through.
556d557f-271a-41d5-ae83-5a7bcb9c32a6: Japan's victory over Russia in 1905 is often described as the first modern defeat of a European great power by an Asian nation, but historian Rotem Kowner cautions against treating the war's outcome as having ______ European imperial dominance. Russia lost a fleet and a war, yet it kept its vast territorial empire, and Britain, France, and other colonial powers held on to their Asian possessions for decades afterward. What the war did change, Kowner argues, was perception: nationalist writers from Cairo to Calcutta cited Japan's success as proof that European supremacy was not inevitable.
55daf2da-8137-464f-93ae-42ba4c47417a: Catalytic converters reduce harmful car exhaust by passing it over thin coatings of metals such as palladium. Molecules of carbon monoxide and unburned hydrocarbons stick briefly to the palladium surface, where they react with oxygen to form less harmful carbon dioxide and water. For decades, engineers assumed that the more palladium a converter contained, the cleaner its output would be. However, chemist Lena Ortiz and her colleagues found that this assumption breaks down when the engine is cold. In their tests, converters with heavy palladium loading performed no better during the first minutes after startup than converters with far less metal, because at low temperatures carbon monoxide molecules crowd the surface so densely that oxygen cannot reach the reactive sites. Ortiz's team concluded that how the palladium is arranged, such as spreading it into tiny, well-separated clusters, matters more for cold-start emissions than how much of it is used.
57baafc1-4549-4a21-8beb-1df144027dd2: In nineteenth-century France, the Academy of Fine Arts ranked painting by subject. History painting—large canvases of mythological, biblical, or heroic scenes—sat at the top, while scenes of ordinary life were considered minor genres suited only to small formats. Gustave Courbet's A Burial at Ornans (1849–1850) deliberately broke this rule. The painting depicts an unremarkable funeral in Courbet's provincial hometown, attended by local villagers, yet it stretches more than six meters wide, the scale traditionally reserved for depictions of gods and kings. When it was shown at the Salon of 1850–1851, many critics condemned it as crude, but they were reacting less to its technique than to the claim its size implied: that the lives of rural laborers were as worthy of monumental treatment as the deeds of emperors.
57f47620-de1c-4f76-b2a4-6e5c03cc6416: From 1932 to 1972, the US Public Health Service conducted a study in Macon County, Alabama, observing hundreds of Black men with syphilis to track the disease's progression. The men were never told their diagnosis; instead, they were offered free meals and medical exams for what researchers called "bad blood." __When penicillin became the standard cure for syphilis in the late 1940s, researchers not only withheld it from participants but also took steps to keep them from receiving it elsewhere.__ Some historians have argued that the study's early years reflected the limited treatments then available, but this later decision undercuts any claim that the project was simply a product of its era's medical knowledge. The study ended only after a whistleblower's account reached the press, prompting reforms that made informed consent a federal requirement.
5836fc83-c89e-4105-9438-a3d8e0a79bff:

58a10ce1-6bbe-477b-ae89-0f0e0e31c668: At the summer fair in Del Río, María spotted her cousin Lucía beside the ring-toss booth. 592aeec2-28ca-4960-acb0-b30f8f0f1cc7: To outside observers, the sema ceremony of the Mevlevi order, founded in thirteenth-century Konya by followers of the poet Rumi, often appears to be a performance of endurance: dancers in tall felt hats and white skirts turn for long stretches without apparent dizziness. Yet for the Ottoman-era dervishes who practiced it, the spinning was valued less as a physical feat than as a structured form of prayer. Each element of the ritual carried assigned meaning. The black cloak removed at the start represented the grave and worldly attachment; the right palm, turned upward, received divine grace, while the left, turned downward, passed that grace to the earth. Even the counterclockwise rotation around the heart was understood as aligning the body with the circling of planets and of pilgrims around the Kaaba. Novices trained for a thousand and one days before joining the ceremony, and much of that training concerned not balance but the inner recitation that was meant to accompany every turn.
5939562e-aa1c-4206-9955-248076f8df65: In electrowetting-on-dielectric (EWOD) devices, tiny droplets sit on a grid of electrodes coated with a thin insulating layer. Applying voltage to the electrode next to a droplet makes that edge of the droplet spread, pulling the whole droplet forward, so chemists can move, merge, and mix reagents without pumps or channels. Engineer Lena Osei suspected that the slow, steady voltage ramps used in most EWOD devices were not needed for reliable movement and that sharp, brief pulses could move droplets just as well while reducing the charge that slowly builds up in the insulating layer and eventually stalls droplets. In her tests with aqueous droplets, pulsed control moved droplets across 2,000 electrode steps with a failure rate no higher than ramped control, and measured charge buildup was about 40 percent lower. __However, when Osei repeated the trials with droplets containing dissolved proteins, which tend to stick to the surface, pulsed control failed to move droplets far more often than ramped control did.__ Osei concludes that pulsed control is a better choice for moving simple aqueous droplets, though not yet for every type of sample used in EWOD chemistry.
5a0b6d12-b8f8-4edf-94db-d50ea8132bad: In thirteenth-century France, poet-composers such as Adam de la Halle wrote songs in a form called the rondeau. 5a538a50-75dd-4c64-8003-cf2996bd8288: Before Bronislaw Malinowski arrived in the Trobriand Islands in 1915, most anthropologists relied on secondhand reports from missionaries and colonial officials. 5aa1b502-22f4-4585-8aba-f47fa1dc7726: For thirty years, Amr and Samir had released their pigeons at dawn from neighboring rooftops in Shubra, watching the flocks circle above the minarets before settling back onto the wire coops. 5b479554-4266-4da8-9f9d-4ab687b1bd41: The Oaths of Strasbourg, sworn in 842 by two grandsons of Charlemagne, are often celebrated as the earliest surviving text in a language recognizably distinct from Latin. Because the chronicler Nithard recorded the oaths in the vernacular each army could understand, the document preserves forms such as "salvar" and "cadhuna," which show sound changes, including the weakening of Latin's final vowels, that had already pulled the spoken Romance of northern Gaul away from its parent tongue. 5b81015b-fde9-4a89-aba8-cb314f5246a1: By the time the steamer rounded the bend below Natchez, Emeline had made up her mind to take the train east. 5c77f652-be57-4bf5-8187-523e42d0be6d: Histories of medieval music often credit the composers of Notre-Dame in Paris, such as Léonin and Pérotin, with transforming plainchant into elaborate polyphony around 1200. Because many of these Chartres fragments were damaged or scattered over the centuries, scholars have only recently begun to compare them systematically with the better-preserved Parisian sources. 5d7d1ccc-7b2d-4a19-a56b-1b4e3e4e58e6: In the opening scene of a novel set at a Louisiana bayou fish camp, six-year-old Baptiste squats at the edge of the marsh grass while his uncles argue over a tangled trotline. 609d26b9-11d9-4505-8981-136df0b7a331: Many companies buy their materials from one business, have another business make their products, and use stores owned by others to sell them. 60b840af-e643-45f9-aae4-8318eb138ddc: Sociologist Erving Goffman used the term "footing" to describe the stance a speaker takes toward their own words, noting that a person may present a statement as their own view or as someone else's. 61be0482-0440-4e31-b9a0-fc9edfe221c6: The Mexican Constitution of 1917 authorized the government to break up large haciendas and grant the land to rural communities as ejidos, holdings that villagers could farm but could not sell. 68c96b60-56b0-4b19-998c-d45a1683adf7: Protein crystallographers have long struggled to grow crystals that are both large and well ordered. 6d26835a-8dbf-46b3-b8e8-792a6d0adc8d: Metal-organic frameworks, or MOFs, are crystals built from metal atoms linked by carbon-based molecules. 6ee76ef5-008d-421a-a80e-9c4e02c4c19b: Because potassium-40 in volcanic minerals decays to argon-40 at a known rate, and because argon gas escapes from molten rock but becomes trapped once crystals form, the potassium-argon method can assign absolute ages to ash layers lying above and below archaeological finds. 72e57111-ddec-48f2-a233-1622151b7d69: In The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life (1956), sociologist Erving Goffman argued that ordinary social encounters resemble theatrical performances: people manage the impressions others form of them, displaying a polished "front stage" self while relaxing in "backstage" regions out of view. 77be6c31-f1c2-4e8f-8ab8-4ed1b77584e1: In the years after the 1917 Russian Revolution, many artists associated with Constructivism argued that painting on canvas was a relic of a private, bourgeois culture and should give way to useful design for posters, books, and buildings. 7ab11dfc-9b65-49b8-a668-cc0cc8a00203: Every week in Mombasa, Kenya, buyers gather to bid on tea grown across East Africa. 7b21363d-18fb-461f-bf4e-9e8bcb7cefa9: According to social comparison theory, first proposed by psychologist Leon Festinger in 1954, people judge their own abilities by measuring themselves against others, especially when no objective standard is available. 7d2a7864-4256-47b1-a73c-36081c47ec15: Filmmakers who adapt Virginia Woolf's novels face a peculiar problem: her narratives unfold less through events than through the drifting thoughts of characters, which slide from memory to perception to fantasy within a single sentence. 7dba0f13-f252-4ad1-a4be-8635f47ba676: When a quartz crystal is squeezed or twisted, the positive and negative ions in its structure shift slightly out of their balanced positions. For decades, climate models treated Arctic permafrost largely as a passive store of carbon, frozen soil that would thaw gradually and release its methane and carbon dioxide at a slow, predictable pace. Field research led by ecologist Merritt Turetsky has complicated that picture. Her team found that in ice-rich permafrost, thawing does not simply proceed downward a few centimeters each year; instead, melting ground ice can cause the land surface to collapse abruptly, forming slumps and ponds known as thermokarst. These waterlogged depressions create oxygen-poor conditions in which microbes produce methane, a greenhouse gas far more potent than carbon dioxide over short periods.

Because the warming caused by this methane can in turn thaw more permafrost, abrupt thaw strengthens a feedback loop that models built around gradual thaw tend to underestimate. Turetsky and her colleagues estimate that although abrupt thaw is likely to affect less than a fifth of the permafrost region, it could roughly double the climate impact projected from gradual thaw alone. Their conclusion is not that the Arctic has already passed a point of no return, but that projections ignoring sudden ground collapse may substantially understate how much permafrost will contribute to future warming.
7efbf956-9ec7-460f-9363-f5d35effd914: Proposed by economists Peter Doeringer and Michael Piore in 1971, the dual labor market hypothesis divides employment into two sectors: a primary sector offering stable jobs, internal promotion ladders, and rising wages, and a secondary sector marked by high turnover and few routes upward. 7fae2c9a-d92e-4975-aafd-ccff37db483e: Popular accounts of the Cuban Missile Crisis of October 1962 often portray it as a contest of nerves won by the side that refused to blink: the United States imposed a naval "quarantine" around Cuba, and the Soviet Union, facing the threat of escalation, withdrew its nuclear missiles from the island. Historians working with declassified records from both governments have complicated this picture. They note that the settlement included terms kept from the public at the time, most notably a private American assurance that Jupiter missiles stationed in Turkey would be removed within months. Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev and President John F. Kennedy, these documents show, also exchanged letters through intermediaries in which each sought a way for the other to retreat without appearing defeated. In this view, the crisis ended less because one leader outlasted the other than because both quietly accepted concessions that allowed each to claim success.
7fc8bd61-52ed-441b-bb86-25cf7696329d: Horace's Ars Poetica, a verse letter written around 19 BCE, offers only scattered advice about drama: a play should have no more and no fewer than five acts, violent deeds are better reported than shown, and a god should not intervene unless the plot truly demands it. Horace presented these remarks casually, often with humor, and never organized them into a system. Yet when Renaissance critics such as Julius Caesar Scaliger and Lodovico Castelvetro rediscovered the poem, they combined its offhand suggestions with passages from Aristotle and recast them as binding laws. By the seventeenth century, French academicians were judging new tragedies largely by how faithfully they observed these "rules," and playwrights such as Pierre Corneille felt compelled to publish essays defending their departures from them. In this way, a loosely composed letter came to shape, for more than two centuries, the standards by which European critics measured a play's structure.
8219c3f4-9396-4e95-ae9f-2ddec85ded65: Researchers testing semiconductor photocatalysts, such as titanium dioxide particles that break down organic pollutants in water when exposed to light, often compare materials by reporting how much of a dye disappears in a fixed time. Chemist Lena Okafor argues that such comparisons can be misleading unless they are based on quantum efficiency: the number of pollutant molecules degraded per photon actually absorbed by the catalyst. A slurry that scatters much of the incoming light, for example, may appear sluggish simply because fewer photons are absorbed, not because the material is chemically inferior. In Okafor's experiments, two catalysts that differed nearly threefold in dye removal per hour turned out to have almost identical quantum efficiencies once the absorbed light in each reactor was measured with chemical actinometry.
82eb774b-da6e-4e6e-b865-e6ea375c6c34: In 1925, anthropologist Margaret Mead traveled to the island of Ta'ū in American Samoa to investigate a question that divided scholars of her era—whether the emotional turmoil of adolescence was a biological inevitability or a product of culture. 83139ebd-7e83-49d5-b864-d9fc325894d8: Perovskite solar cells have attracted attention because they can be made cheaply from solutions rather than from the ultrapure silicon wafers that conventional panels require. That low-temperature processing, however, leaves the crystals riddled with defects, such as missing ions and misaligned grain boundaries. Researchers long assumed these flaws would trap electrons and sharply reduce efficiency, as similar defects do in silicon. Yet perovskite cells routinely convert more than 25 percent of sunlight into electricity. Studies by materials physicists suggest an explanation: most of the common defects in perovskites create energy states that lie very close to the edges of the material's energy bands rather than deep within the gap between them. Electrons that fall into such shallow states can easily escape again, so the defects do little to hinder the flow of current. The material, in other words, appears to be unusually tolerant of its own imperfections.

862d879e-363f-4a1a-abe6-c38a9b211b4c: The phrase "triangular trade" is often used to describe Atlantic commerce from the sixteenth to the nineteenth centuries: European manufactured goods shipped to West Africa, enslaved Africans carried across the Atlantic to the Americas, and sugar, tobacco, and cotton returned to Europe. Historians such as David Eltis, however, have argued that the triangle misrepresents how most voyages actually operated. Shipping records show that many vessels did not complete all three legs; ships that delivered captives to the Caribbean frequently sailed home with little cargo, while plantation goods crossed the ocean on separate, specialized ships. Moreover, a large share of the trade to Brazil ran directly between Brazilian and African ports, with tobacco and rum from Bahia exchanged for captives in Angola and the Bight of Benin, bypassing Europe entirely. For these historians, the system is better understood as a web of overlapping routes than as a single closed loop.
863e7612-4d17-46ed-8424-3e44462e414a: When titanium dioxide absorbs ultraviolet light, electrons in the material are boosted to a higher energy level, leaving behind positively charged "holes." 867c8976-d89a-477e-9428-594f68cc76c4: When Madame Rousseau pried loose the cracked hinge of the jewelry box, a walnut case the pawnbroker had wrapped carelessly in yesterday's newspaper, she found what the damage had long kept hidden______ someone had etched a column of tiny dates, each one falling within the years of the Occupation, beside a pair of initials that were not her late husband's.
871c51d3-e90d-4e68-870c-97eece119659: Each winter, a team of herpetologists surveying a cluster of vernal pools in northern California reported that Pacific chorus frogs (Pseudacris regilla) at the site were thriving: on the first rainy nights of the season, hundreds of males gathered and called in near-perfect synchrony, and females laid thousands of eggs within a span of about ten days. 88fc97e0-554c-4aab-ab08-221b3ea2d4a5: For much of the twentieth century, art historians told the story of Western art mainly through the careers of celebrated male painters, treating women artists as rare exceptions. 894d98b8-cf3d-49ec-94c9-cc3410bab3b2: After French soldiers unearthed the Rosetta Stone in 1799, scholars raced to read its hieroglyphic section by comparing it with the stone's Greek translation. 8b94694f-3f4a-4622-86e1-b928eb6431bd: The Implicit Association Test (IAT) asks participants to sort faces and words as quickly as possible, and in one version Black and White faces share response keys with positive or negative words. 8e78cd81-0050-4347-8100-85f183c4ce07: The following text is adapted from a short story. 93d5b887-9c38-4947-b88b-c1cc68735c45: In his treatises on Noh theatre, the fifteenth-century actor and playwright Zeami Motokiyo praised moments he described as "where nothing is done." Text 1
Some critics argue that Primo Levi's If This Is a Man succeeds mainly because it avoids literary technique. In their view, Levi simply recorded events at Auschwitz in the order they happened, like a witness giving plain testimony in court, and the book's power comes from this lack of shaping.

Text 2
Levi's memoir is often praised as plain testimony, but its structure was carefully designed. Levi arranged many chapters around themes, such as language or exchange in the camp, rather than strict chronology. He also chose which scenes to expand and which to compress. This deliberate shaping is a key reason the book affects readers so deeply.
94ae5a26-f5ae-4e3c-9ae3-6fa32aeac44a: Crystalline silicon dominates the solar-panel market, yet its physics imposes a firm ceiling on performance. Silicon's band gap—the minimum energy an electron must absorb to break free and carry current—is about 1.1 electron volts. Photons carrying less energy than this pass through the material without freeing electrons at all. __Photons carrying more energy, such as those in blue light, do free electrons, but any energy beyond the band gap is quickly shed as heat rather than converted to electricity.__ Because sunlight contains a broad mix of photon energies, these two losses together mean that even a flawless single-junction silicon cell cannot convert much more than about 30 percent of incoming sunlight into electrical power.
94f3c2e3-244c-4971-b762-1c9a2bf4ffc1: The Pacific lamprey, a jawless fish that spends part of its adult life at sea, feeds by fastening its round, tooth-lined oral disc to the side of a larger fish and rasping through the skin with its tongue. Because each compound targets a different stage, the host cannot easily compensate by strengthening any single defense, and blood keeps flowing for the hours or even days that the lamprey remains attached.
969287e7-6ab6-4d38-a9e9-a145d7904363: Many buildings overheat in the afternoon and cool too quickly at night. b5f3a97b-7535-4e99-a88c-d1fa653e140b: When propylene is polymerized with a Ziegler-Natta catalyst, the resulting polypropylene is usually isotactic: nearly every methyl group along the chain points to the same side, which lets the chains pack into rigid crystals. A competing hypothesis, advanced by researchers studying titanium chloride catalysts, holds that control comes from the chiral geometry of the metal site itself: the asymmetric arrangement of atoms around each titanium center lets an incoming propylene molecule bind in only one orientation, no matter how the chain attached to that site happens to be arranged.
b6e980d3-3ca7-4ad2-9aa6-7d1123cef098: In the late nineteenth century, physicists observed that certain metals release electrons when struck by ultraviolet light. b6ee246c-b2be-476e-8bce-0d0d4923cc41: For decades after its introduction in 1950, the F-scale, a questionnaire designed to measure "authoritarian personality" traits such as rigid deference to authority and hostility toward outsiders, was treated as a reliable predictor of both obedience and prejudice. Most of the supporting evidence, however, came from surveys of white, middle-class respondents in the United States. When social psychologist Anika Brandt and colleagues administered a revised version of the scale to adults in eleven countries, they found that high scorers everywhere tended to report greater willingness to follow orders from superiors. The link between high scores and prejudice, by contrast, varied sharply: it was strong in some samples but nearly absent in others, particularly where the groups regarded as outsiders were themselves favored by local authorities.

b77254bf-cf1e-407c-a92b-72487e0c0ba1: Psychologists studying moral licensing have found that people who have recently done something virtuous sometimes feel freer to act selfishly afterward, as though their good deed had earned them credit to spend. b7c1107c-cf32-4f37-9e9e-b1817200dcbf: Retailers once cut prices on seasonal stock according to fixed calendars, marking down every item by the same percentage on the same date. b7cb0820-ea0c-417c-8c73-d64c7914aa38: Each evening, after the last of the well water had been rationed among the hogs and the kitchen garden, Ernst carried a dented pail to the lean-to behind the barn. b813eb91-6efc-4d80-8631-10e987928c3e: Psychologist Melvin Lerner proposed that many people hold an unspoken belief that the world is fair: good things happen to good people, and bad things happen to those who somehow deserve them. b8a22bd6-9beb-499b-8012-47df6d603d45: Historians often credit Johannes Gutenberg's movable-type press, developed in Mainz around 1440, with placing books in the hands of ordinary Europeans for the first time. The claim has some basis: by 1500, presses across Europe had produced millions of volumes, and the cost of a book fell sharply compared with that of a hand-copied manuscript. __Yet surviving sales records show that most early printed books were Latin religious and legal texts, priced well beyond the means of the farmers and laborers who made up the majority of the population.__ For several generations, then, the press mainly enlarged the libraries of clergy, lawyers, and wealthy merchants. Only later, as cheap pamphlets and vernacular works multiplied, did printing begin to reach readers outside these groups.
b94c1469-5fa9-4ea1-a5f4-fba1da245127: In the early 1950s, psychologist Solomon Asch asked participants to match the length of a reference line to one of three comparison lines, a task so simple that people tested alone almost never erred. b9933038-a847-4540-9bc5-ba3dcf149f17:
Text 1
In Lucia Ferrante's novel The Stoop on Sackett Street, set in 1910s Brooklyn, Rosa watches from her tenement stoop as her younger sister, Nina, leaves to board a steamer for California. Nina calls up to her twice, but Rosa says nothing and only raises a hand. Critic Daniel Ames argues that this wordless moment is the emotional center of the book. In his view, Rosa's refusal to speak shows a longing to escape that she cannot admit, and the scene therefore shows that the novel treats family duty as a trap that silences immigrant daughters.

Text 2
Scholar Teresa Valli also considers the departure scene central to Ferrante's novel, but she points out how Rosa behaves elsewhere in the book. When Rosa turns down a suitor who offers to take her to Chicago, and again when she agrees to run her father's fruit stand, she also says nothing. In both cases, the narrator describes her afterward as "settled" and "at ease." Valli concludes that in Ferrante's novel, Rosa falls silent when she has made a choice she accepts, not when she is hiding a regret.
ba02b681-33e2-49d9-9e6b-f8eb039ab5ea: Samir crossed half of Cairo with a single gray pigeon tucked inside his shirt. The bird had escaped weeks earlier and somehow flown back to his coop, and now he meant to return it to Laila, the girl who had named it years before. bb23925a-79bc-4d37-a475-d90fce06f351: In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, much Swiss watchmaking ran on a cottage system. Merchants sent parts to farm families in the Jura Mountains, and each district specialized in a single stage of production: some valleys made rough movements, while workshops in Geneva finished cases and dials. It might seem that spreading production across so many households would have multiplied expenses. Economic historians argue, however, that the arrangement did not add to merchants' costs; instead, concentrating each task in one district ______ those costs. Neighbors shared specialized tools, trained one another's apprentices, and sent finished parts only short distances.
bb438057-50f3-49b0-a9da-a71acf1aa483: In 1494, envoys of Spain and Portugal signed the Treaty of Tordesillas, which drew a north-south line roughly 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands and assigned newly encountered lands east of it to Portugal and those west of it to Spain. The agreement is often remembered as a bold carving-up of the globe, but its authors understood remarkably little of what they were dividing. No one in 1494 could reliably measure longitude at sea, so neither crown could say exactly where the line fell, and the treaty itself left the matter to a future joint expedition that never took place. Within a few years, Portuguese navigators reached the coast of what is now Brazil and argued it lay on their side; decades later, the two kingdoms quarreled over whether the Moluccas, the prized spice islands, fell within Portugal's or Spain's sphere once the line was extended around the far side of the world. Thus a treaty meant to settle rivalry instead supplied the vocabulary in which new rivalries were argued.
bc97941e-7045-46e4-83aa-6463d2912a46: For much of the twentieth century, Finland's paper and pulp companies outcompeted rivals in countries with far larger forests. Economists often attribute this success to vertical integration: firms such as UPM and Stora Enso came to control every stage of production, from timber harvesting to sawmills, pulp plants, and paper machines. __Yet integration alone cannot explain the industry's durability, since Swedish and Canadian firms adopted similar structures without matching Finland's consistency over decades.__ Historian Markku Kuisma points instead to the country's forest management regime, under which hundreds of thousands of small private landowners, guided by state-funded advisers, replanted harvested land on predictable cycles. This steady, renewable timber supply, Kuisma argues, is what allowed integrated mills to operate at full capacity year after year.
bdd63240-cb6c-4dd1-81b9-494780475ee9: In January 1968, Alexander Dubček became leader of Czechoslovakia's Communist Party and soon announced a program he called "socialism with a human face." Press censorship was relaxed, citizens openly debated the party's past abuses, and reformers drafted plans to allow greater economic independence for enterprises. Many historians have described these months, later known as the Prague Spring, as an attempt to abandon communism altogether. __Yet the party's own Action Program of April 1968 explicitly reaffirmed Czechoslovakia's membership in the Warsaw Pact and the Communist Party's leading role in society.__ Soviet leaders nonetheless viewed the reforms as a threat to their control of Eastern Europe, and in August 1968 Warsaw Pact troops invaded the country, ending the experiment within a single night.
be0a77c0-72ed-4f0c-9166-b021571d3706: When a volcano erupts explosively, it sends a tall column of ash into the sky. Scientists use computer programs called dispersion models to predict where that ash will travel and how far from the volcano it will fall to the ground. These models combine information about the height of the ash column, the size of the ash particles, and the speed and direction of the wind at different altitudes. Large, heavy particles tend to drop out close to the volcano, while fine particles can be carried hundreds of kilometers away. By running these models, scientists can warn airports, farms, and towns about where ash is likely to land, giving people time to prepare.
be1276fa-bb0b-4ccb-bb24-3a3d49a55e31: From his seat beside the tram window, Senhor Oliveira had watched the Saints' procession wind down Rua da Graça for fifty-one Junes. This year, a spark from a paper lantern caught the hem of a small boy's Saint Anthony costume, and the crowd, a tangle of grandmothers, fishmongers, and brass-band players who had been singing together only moments earlier, ______ neighbors shoved past neighbors, and no one seemed certain whose child the boy was.
bee1f906-ebed-42be-a0f8-b1fa68a2e096: In the early 1900s, inspectors at American silk mills routinely judged the best Italian raw silk to be finer and more lustrous, skein for skein, than anything arriving from Japan. Yet over the same decades, those mills shifted their purchases decisively toward Japanese silk, which Japanese cooperatives had begun sorting by standardized cocoon grades so that every bale of a given grade matched the others closely. ______ the factor that won American buyers was evidently not the excellence of any single skein but the assurance that thread from one shipment would run on high-speed power looms just like thread from the last.

Karim lifted his hides from the vat, and the indigo ran off them like evening sky. Hassan barely looked. "Your blue is muddy again," he said. c0020627-224d-4495-8ad8-57a8a6472b35: Every morning Giorgi still unlocked the schoolhouse at the edge of the village, a squat stone building whose stove no one had lit since the last family left for Tbilisi. c04a5d02-86db-4452-bc25-2f61e61bbbc7: The lotus leaf stays remarkably dry even in heavy rain. c175e2ce-634a-48e5-a3c5-fc25207c0cf6: After the Great Fire of 1666 destroyed most of the City of London, Christopher Wren was commissioned to rebuild more than fifty parish churches. Many of the sites he inherited were cramped, irregular plots hemmed in by surviving houses and lanes, so a single standard plan was impossible. Rather than forcing a uniform design onto each lot, Wren treated every church as a separate problem, fitting naves into odd angles and placing entrances wherever the street allowed. Yet he held firmly to one priority across these varied buildings: that the congregation should be able to see the pulpit and hear the preacher clearly. Wren argued that a Protestant church was essentially an "auditory," a room for listening, and he kept interiors compact and largely free of obstructing columns. The striking towers and steeples that rose above the rooftops, often designed years after the main structures were finished, gave each church a distinctive public face, but the logic of the interior began with the spoken word.

c2118896-b216-4873-b633-60c06a7b22e1: Like most liquids, motor oil becomes thinner as its temperature rises, which can leave hot engine parts poorly protected. c21ab1ec-fa06-4666-b9b3-cfb63f02f6c2: When ceramic powders are heated to make solid parts, two things happen at once: the tiny particles fuse together and the gaps between them close, a process called densification, and the small crystals, or grains, inside the material slowly grow larger. c2ee2c52-0738-4570-8ee2-43ca23116343: In the 1830s, Scottish chemist Thomas Graham, who had already shown that a gas's rate of effusion is inversely proportional to the square root of its molar mass, turned to a harder question: how quickly two different gases mix with each other. c48637e5-c7f2-466e-8309-55524b577638: Richard Wagner believed that opera should be a Gesamtkunstwerk, or "total work of art," in which music, poetry, and stage design merged into a single dramatic experience. Many historians argue that the printing press made the Protestant Reformation possible. Text 2
Printed Bibles were important, but they were also expensive, and most sixteenth-century Europeans could not read. c815dddc-391f-4039-a14f-16d9de4aa114: Japan's Tokugawa shogunate issued a series of edicts between 1633 and 1639 that barred most Japanese from traveling abroad, expelled Portuguese traders, and confined Dutch merchants to the tiny artificial island of Dejima in Nagasaki harbor. cd3c70bc-12e8-4230-a371-07777539ee04: Open-cell polymer foams are widely used to absorb sound, but engineers disagree about which mechanism accounts for most of the energy they remove from an incoming wave. One view holds that the dominant loss comes from viscous friction: as air is forced back and forth through the narrow, interconnected pores, it rubs against the pore walls and its kinetic energy is converted to heat. Materials scientist Leena Okafor proposes an alternative. She argues that in foams with relatively flexible struts, the dominant loss instead comes from the solid skeleton itself, which flexes with each pressure cycle and dissipates energy internally, so that the stiffness of the foam's frame—not the size of its pores—chiefly determines how much sound it absorbs.

ce71df12-711d-45b1-924b-72cb911f1da6:
The idea that the words a language provides can shape how its speakers perceive the world, often associated with linguists Edward Sapir and Benjamin Lee Whorf, has been tested most rigorously in the domain of color. Russian, for example, uses two basic terms, "siniy" and "goluboy," for darker and lighter blues, whereas English uses only "blue." In a 2007 study, Jonathan Winawer and colleagues found that Russian speakers were faster than English speakers at telling apart two blues that fell on opposite sides of the siniy-goluboy boundary.

Yet the researchers also observed that this advantage disappeared when participants were asked to silently repeat a string of digits while performing the task, an activity that occupies verbal memory. Because Russian speakers' eyes did not change during the digit task, the result suggests that the language advantage depends on speakers actively drawing on their color words in the moment rather than on any permanent difference in how they see. Findings like these have led many researchers to favor a modest version of the hypothesis over the claim that language fixes the limits of perception.
d011f6b9-94fe-4c83-a346-ddcc9ac87777: On the first day of her forecasting seminar, meteorologist Dana Ruiz told her students that the high-pressure system parked over their region was "the dullest weather there is": sinking air, clear skies, and light winds spiraling clockwise outward from the center, as the Coriolis effect dictates in the Northern Hemisphere. She then asked them to record surface conditions beneath the system every morning for a week. By Friday, their logs showed dense valley fog at dawn and steadily rising levels of particulate pollution, both trapped under the layer of warm, sinking air that the system maintained. Ruiz had not predicted either outcome aloud, but weeks earlier she had already scheduled Friday's session as a lecture titled "Hazards of Calm."
d0f2fd79-8e37-4785-ade7-8d65eaf0a61a: Accounts of the Boxer Rebellion (1899–1901) often present it as a simple outburst of hatred toward foreigners. Historian Joseph Esherick, however, traced the movement's origins to the drought-stricken villages of northwestern Shandong province. There, Christian converts sometimes relied on the legal protection of foreign missionaries to win local land and lawsuit disputes. Unemployed young men, idled by failed harvests, blamed both the drought and their worsening circumstances on these converts and their foreign patrons. Esherick argues that the Boxers' hostility toward outsiders, though real, grew out of specific local grievances rather than a long-standing, nationwide rejection of everything foreign.
d2756c2b-d7ad-4a91-94e5-ce945aa7b378: In 1968, psychologist Robert Rosenthal and school principal Lenore Jacobson reported the results of a study at an elementary school in California. At the start of the school year, students took a test that the researchers described to teachers as a measure of who was likely to "bloom" intellectually. The researchers then told teachers which students had scored as likely bloomers. In fact, those students had been chosen at random and did not differ from their classmates. When the students were tested again months later, the randomly labeled children, especially those in the earliest grades, showed larger gains in IQ scores than their peers did. Rosenthal and Jacobson concluded that the teachers' beliefs about the students had somehow translated into real differences in how much the students improved.
d32f9605-20b9-4dd4-81f7-51e440dc2996: In 1973, psychologist David Rosenhan published a study in which eight mentally healthy volunteers sought admission to psychiatric hospitals by claiming to hear voices. Once admitted, they stopped reporting any symptoms and behaved normally, yet staff kept them for an average of nineteen days, and nearly all were discharged with a diagnosis of schizophrenia "in remission." Rosenhan argued that the hospital setting itself shaped how staff read behavior: one pseudopatient's habit of taking notes, for instance, was recorded in his chart as "engaging in writing behavior." __Notably, several actual patients on the wards voiced suspicions that the volunteers were journalists or researchers rather than people who were ill.__ For Rosenhan, this contrast suggested that the difficulty lay less in the volunteers' behavior than in the expectations that came with an institutional label.
d412ef3a-f02d-40b2-b432-1ed869ac6ba8:

d41bb66c-c39e-48ec-9d6f-9f627a059c89: A widely circulated television segment from the 1960s showed an unsuspecting person stepping into an elevator, only to turn and face the back wall after several actors did so. The clip is often cited as proof that people will copy strangers even when the behavior makes no sense. When psychologist Maren Ostby and her colleagues staged forty modern versions of the scenario in office buildings, however, they found a more qualified pattern. Riders who were alone with the actors frequently turned around, but riders who entered with a friend almost never did, and many laughed or commented on the odd behavior. Ostby concludes that the original segment did capture a genuine tendency to follow a group, but that this tendency weakens sharply once a person has even one ally whose behavior differs from the group's.
d43954ee-e92c-467d-91c8-f823ae486ab7: Graphene, a single layer of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal lattice, conducts electricity remarkably well in laboratory samples, but the methods used to make it in large quantities tend to undermine that property. The cheapest approach, chemically peeling apart graphite and then removing the oxygen added during the process, yields large amounts of material, yet the resulting flakes are riddled with holes and leftover oxygen groups that scatter electrons. Materials scientist Priya Raman and her colleagues reasoned that the defects themselves might be repaired after production rather than avoided beforehand. They exposed chemically produced graphene to a brief pulse of intense microwave radiation, which heated the flakes to over 2,000°C in about two seconds. The treatment drove off most of the remaining oxygen and allowed carbon atoms to resettle into an orderly lattice, raising the material's conductivity nearly to that of graphene grown by slower, far more expensive vapor-deposition methods.
d50ee4a0-2781-4916-ba36-533e54ce503f: African lungfish survive seasonal droughts by burrowing into the mud of drying riverbeds and secreting a mucus cocoon around their bodies, a dormant state known as estivation. Researchers long assumed that the fish endured these months simply by drawing down stored energy at a normal pace until the rains returned. Measurements of oxygen consumption in estivating lungfish, however, tell a different story: the fish lower their metabolic rate to a small fraction of its usual level, and genes involved in tissue repair and protection against cellular damage become more active. Rather than passively waiting out the drought, the lungfish appears to shift its body into a distinct, actively regulated state that conserves energy while guarding its organs against harm.
d5541b95-1898-40a2-bdf9-5bc46912ed88: In microfluidic devices, liquids travel through channels narrower than a human hair. At such tiny scales, viscosity matters far more than inertia, so the fluid moves in smooth, parallel layers instead of swirling ______ two streams flowing side by side in the same channel barely mix at all.
d62501e3-6de2-4258-ad9e-bcfa7f6aaf5a: In the southern Indian city of Tiruppur, often called the knitwear capital of Tamil Nadu, few firms handle every stage of production under one roof. Instead, work moves among hundreds of specialized workshops. Relying on dense networks of small subcontractors for dyeing, printing, and stitching, ______ able to fill large overseas orders far faster than a single vertically integrated factory could.
d6472b7a-a28c-4e27-8d88-8cb10227ec8d: In the late 1500s, Spanish colonial officials in Peru forced Indigenous workers to labor in the silver mines of Potosí through a system called the mita. Workers were paid wages far below what they needed to survive, and many had to rely on their families to send food. Historians argue that these low wages were not accidental: officials deliberately kept pay ______ so that more of the mines' wealth would flow to Spain.
d66f85ff-f898-44bc-be54-3f4eb590b027: In the 1980s, political scientist James Flynn compiled decades of intelligence test data from more than a dozen developed nations and found that average raw scores had risen by roughly three points per decade. Because the gains appeared in countries with very different school systems and economies, Flynn argued that they could not be ______ to any single national policy; instead, he proposed that broad shifts in modern life, such as greater exposure to abstract classification tasks, had gradually changed how people approach test questions.
d69b18fc-ecea-4f73-8aad-3a4589245ad4: In her 1983 book The Managed Heart, sociologist Arlie Russell Hochschild examined how flight attendants were trained to produce warmth on demand, smiling through turbulence and rude passengers alike. Her central concept, emotional labor, describes the effort workers expend to display the feelings that their employers ______ the hidden cost of this effort, Hochschild argued, is often a growing sense of estrangement from one's own emotions.
d79292a0-c566-4fbe-b9fe-46f05a04775a: In 1962, linguist William Labov wanted to know whether the way New Yorkers pronounced the "r" sound in words like "fourth" and "floor" was linked to social class. Instead of interviewing people formally, he visited three Manhattan department stores that served shoppers of different income levels: Saks Fifth Avenue, Macy's, and S. Klein. In each store, he asked employees where a certain item could be found, knowing that the answer would be "fourth floor." __He found that workers at Saks pronounced the "r" most often, workers at Macy's less often, and workers at S. Klein least often.__ Labov concluded that pronunciation in the city followed a pattern tied to social standing.
d929bf0d-7dd3-489a-abc5-7c44611cb2e9: Engineers protecting buildings from earthquakes have long relied on passive dampers, devices filled with oil that resist motion by a fixed amount. Such dampers work well for the shaking they were designed for but cannot adjust when an earthquake proves stronger or weaker than expected. Magnetorheological (MR) dampers offer an alternative. They contain a fluid with suspended iron particles; when an electromagnetic coil inside the damper is switched on, the particles line up into chains, and the fluid thickens from a liquid with the consistency of motor oil to something close to a soft solid within milliseconds. By varying the current, sensors and a controller can tune the damper's resistance as ground motion changes. Because the coil needs only about as much power as a household light bulb, MR dampers can keep running on backup batteries even when an earthquake knocks out the electrical grid. This is an important advantage, since the stronger kinds of adjustable systems need large power supplies that may fail at exactly the moment they are needed.
d9a578a9-cb93-4217-bd03-7c24095bf322: For centuries, violinists and collectors have claimed that instruments made by Antonio Stradivari in the early 1700s possess a tone no modern maker can match, and many researchers have tried to explain this supposed superiority through the materials he used. One popular hypothesis holds that the spruce for his soundboards grew during a period of unusually cold European winters, producing dense, evenly spaced growth rings that would vibrate with exceptional clarity. Yet when acoustician Claudia Fritz and her colleagues asked experienced soloists to play both old Italian violins and high-quality new ones while wearing modified goggles that hid each instrument's identity, the players could not reliably tell the two groups apart, and several actually preferred a new violin. These results suggest that the celebrated sound of a Stradivarius may owe less to its wood than to the expectations listeners and players bring to it.
da6c792a-7fb2-4e0e-af03-a452cec48771: Anthropologist Mary Douglas developed a framework, known as grid-group analysis, to explain why people in different communities judge dangers so differently. "Group" describes how strongly a person feels bound to a larger community, while "grid" describes how much a person's life is shaped by fixed rules and roles. __For example, members of a tightly knit religious commune with few formal ranks would score high on group but low on grid.__ Douglas argued that a person's position on these two dimensions helps predict which risks, such as pollution or economic collapse, that person will worry about most.
db095b17-90a1-49fc-9b42-0cd61b999d22: Anthropologist Victor Turner observed that in many societies, initiation rites include a "liminal" phase in which participants have left their old social position but not yet entered a new one. db5ca9e9-8444-4e59-bed2-0bb3074b2e77: Popular accounts of "tipping points" in crime, influenced by Malcolm Gladwell, suggest that once disorder in a neighborhood passes some critical level, offending spreads rapidly from person to person, much like a contagious illness. dc0d5b8a-e57d-4d4d-9867-e363c1a0fe13: When a laser beam strikes a sample, a tiny fraction of the scattered photons shifts in energy by amounts that correspond to the vibrations of the sample's chemical bonds. dcd983fc-2c1c-4aea-8982-002b18b652c2: When lava cools into basalt, tiny grains of magnetite inside the rock lock in the direction of Earth's magnetic field at that moment. In the mid-twentieth century, geologists sampling stacked lava flows in places such as Iceland and Hawaii noticed that some layers recorded a field pointing roughly north, as it does today, while others recorded one pointing south. At first, some researchers suspected that certain minerals simply magnetized themselves backward as they cooled, a chemical quirk unrelated to the planet's field. That explanation weakened when scientists dated the flows using the slow decay of radioactive potassium into argon. Rocks of the same age from distant continents turned out to share the same polarity, and reversed layers did not consistently contain a different mix of minerals than normal ones. By matching polarity to age across many sites, researchers assembled a timeline of alternating normal and reversed intervals—the geomagnetic polarity timescale—which later helped confirm that the seafloor spreads outward from mid-ocean ridges.
de32934f-d26c-49d9-8368-337f4c74154d: In the early twentieth century, the mining company LKAB built Kiruna, a town in Sweden's far north, to house the workers who extracted its iron ore. Historians have often assumed that such arrangements left workers with little bargaining power. __Yet Kiruna's miners organized one of the longest strikes in modern Swedish history in 1969–1970, winning concessions on pay structure and working conditions without the backing of their national union.__ Some scholars now argue that the town's very isolation and the shared dependence of residents on a single employer fostered a tight solidarity that made such collective action possible.
def558e8-12cc-4926-afae-bafebc01b9ab: For eleven years, tram conductor Neves had considered the passenger Vitor a know-it-all who could not stop criticizing how she drove the old No. 28 car up the hills of Lisbon. dfbc94c2-22a4-49bf-8298-19a9825f218f: In early Occitan troubadour poetry of the twelfth century, the word "fin'amor" (refined love) described a lover's devotion to a noble lady, often a married woman of high rank. e1fd30fb-bfc5-4ecf-bc6e-ff9c00f82dd6: In her 2010 performance The Artist Is Present, Marina Abramović sat silently in a chair at the Museum of Modern Art for more than seven hundred hours. e201f9eb-b827-4eac-a0dc-c3fa199c11d1: When Japanese woodblock prints began reaching Paris in the 1860s, many European collectors prized them chiefly as exotic curiosities, admiring their bright, flat colors. Yet the painters who studied them most closely, among them Edgar Degas and Claude Monet, were drawn less to the prints' novelty than to the way artists such as Katsushika Hokusai organized space. In Hokusai's series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, the famous peak is often pushed to the margins or shrunk to a small triangle behind a towering wave or a cooper's barrel, while foreground objects are abruptly cropped by the edge of the sheet. Such choices broke with the European convention, inherited from Renaissance linear perspective, of placing the principal subject at the center of a balanced, deep scene. Degas's off-center dancers, sliced by the frame, and Monet's high horizons suggest that these painters found in ukiyo-e not a style to imitate but a model for rethinking how a picture could be composed.
e39f4c82-d4db-43cb-92c2-d84232c82d64:
Text 1
Some Western listeners describe Hindustani raags as simply "scales," like the major and minor scales of European music. On this view, once a listener learns which notes a raag uses, the listener understands the raag well enough to follow any performance of it.

Text 2
A raag is more than a set of notes. Two raags can share exactly the same notes yet sound completely different, because each has its own rules about which notes to stress, how to glide between them, and which phrases to repeat. Musicians learn these rules through years of study within the tradition, so knowing the notes alone tells a listener very little.
e4075607-7e49-43b9-b79a-99d28da5d96b: In Stanley Milgram's obedience experiments of the early 1960s, volunteers were told to give what they believed were increasingly strong electric shocks to another person whenever that person answered a question wrongly. Many participants kept going while an experimenter calmly urged them on, and this result is often summarized as proof that ordinary people will obey any authority. Later analyses of Milgram's own records point to a narrower conclusion. Obedience fell sharply when the experimenter gave instructions by telephone, when two other "teachers" refused to continue, and when the study was moved from Yale University to a shabby office building. Also, when the experimenter said outright, "You have no other choice, you must go on," almost every participant who heard it stopped. Participants seemed willing to continue mainly when they could see themselves as helping a legitimate scientific project, not when they were simply being given orders.
e49f18af-6443-46ce-9ac1-84b1c7527700: Speakers of Guugu Yimithirr, an Aboriginal language of northeastern Australia, describe locations almost entirely with cardinal directions, saying in effect "the cup is north of the plate" rather than "the cup is to the left of the plate." Some researchers have argued that such habits shape how speakers mentally encode space. In one well-known task, participants viewed a row of objects on a table, were turned 180 degrees to face a second table, and were asked to rebuild the row "the same way." Dutch speakers, whose language relies on left and right, usually kept the row's order relative to their own bodies, whereas Guugu Yimithirr speakers usually kept its compass orientation. Critics have noted, however, that the two groups also differed in setting: most Guugu Yimithirr participants lived in rural areas with strong outdoor landmarks, while the Dutch participants were mostly city dwellers tested indoors. Later studies that compared speakers of different languages living in the same environment have found that language still predicts which strategy people choose, although environment influences that choice too.
e5346354-c08f-4e8b-997b-623f76eba733: Historians reconstructing the Armenian genocide of 1915 have often relied on the testimony of survivors and foreign diplomats, sources that Ottoman officials at the time dismissed as exaggerated or hostile. In recent decades, however, researchers such as Taner Akçam have turned to the Ottoman state's own records, including coded telegrams exchanged between the Interior Ministry and provincial governors. These documents show officials tracking the number of Armenians deported from each district and ordering that the deportees' share of the population in their destination regions be kept below a fixed percentage. __Such instructions are difficult to reconcile with the government's wartime claim that the deportations were merely a temporary security measure to move civilians away from the front lines.__ Instead, the records suggest a deliberate demographic policy, one whose execution through forced marches into the Syrian desert led to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of civilians.
e6900279-7470-40e2-b0a2-04d7b9bb8627: Conventional polymerase chain reaction (PCR), which copies DNA so that trace amounts can be detected, typically requires benchtop thermal cyclers and sample volumes measured in tens of microliters. Engineers developing microfluidic "lab-on-a-chip" devices have shown that splitting a sample into thousands of picoliter droplets, each heated and cooled as it moves through channels etched in a chip, can ______ this process: the same amplification occurs, but in a device small enough to hold in one hand and with each cycle finishing in seconds rather than minutes.
e7365553-43fa-48fb-be94-e9066414f776: Inside a narrow glass tube, water climbs upward and forms a concave meniscus because its molecules adhere to the glass more strongly than they cohere to one another. Mercury, whose atoms are held together by cohesive forces far stronger than any attraction they feel toward glass______ in the opposite way: its surface bulges into a convex dome, and its level sinks below that of the surrounding liquid.
e7f9cf9d-c776-4eb0-8bb3-bacfe94cd8fb:
Text 1
In Marisol Abad's novel The Tide Schedule, the aging teacher Mr. Reyes spends forty years competing with Mr. Dalisay, the younger teacher on the island's school boat. Near the end, Reyes quietly hands Dalisay his worn lesson ledger. Critic Lorna Vibal reads this as surrender: with retirement near, Reyes gives up the rivalry that has defined him and admits that Dalisay has won.

Text 2
Critic Ben Aquino points out that Reyes's ledger is not a clean record of his own lessons. Its margins are full of notes reacting to Dalisay's methods: "D. tried this with fractions—better," "Answer D.'s tide-chart lesson next week." Aquino argues that for decades each man built his teaching partly in reply to the other, so their rivalry worked as a long, unspoken collaboration.
e80cc851-7156-45f6-92c4-8c3d5022783c: Western viewers encountering Song dynasty landscape scrolls have often judged them to lack perspective, since the paintings contain no single vanishing point toward which lines converge. Yet the eleventh-century painter and theorist Guo Xi described three distinct kinds of distance—looking up at a peak from its base, peering from the front of a mountain into the valleys behind it, and gazing across level ground toward far-off hills—and he urged painters to combine all three within one composition. __Such a combination is impossible for an observer fixed in one spot, because each view requires the eye to stand somewhere different.__ A Song scroll, then, does not fail to achieve a single coherent viewpoint; it deliberately sets that viewpoint aside so that the viewer can wander through the landscape as if traveling within it, experiencing distance without being held at a distance.

e8bbd987-b3b5-4cb3-870e-22f0ceab7d44: When the Philippine-American War began in 1899, many US commanders expected Filipino resistance to collapse once Emilio Aguinaldo's conventional army was defeated in open battle. Historians therefore argue that the war's most consequential phase began, rather than ended, with the breakup of the Filipino regular army.
ea7b7e9c-c4c6-418a-9600-3a14caa57b89: In the late 1970s, anthropologist Catherine Lutz lived on Ifaluk, a small atoll in Micronesia. She found that its residents sorted feelings into categories that do not line up neatly with the English words often treated as universal. For example, Ifaluk speakers use the word song for a kind of justified, morally charged anger. It is directed at someone who has broken a community rule, especially a rule about sharing food and labor. Lutz noticed that this emotion word is used most often in the same settings where duties to share are strongest. From this, she argued that a community's social arrangements actively shape which emotion categories its members recognize and use, rather than people everywhere starting from a fixed set of basic emotions.
ebadc416-94b1-4991-9e62-d153a262aa52: For much of the twentieth century, editors of Emily Dickinson's poems quietly "corrected" her manuscripts, replacing her many dashes with commas and periods and lowering her idiosyncratic capital letters. Their assumption was that these marks were careless habits of private writing, not deliberate choices. __Yet when scholar Thomas H. Johnson restored the original markings in his 1955 edition, readers found that a single dash could hold two clauses in suspension, letting a line be read as both the end of one thought and the beginning of another.__ Later critics built on this observation, arguing that Dickinson's capitals similarly elevate ordinary nouns—"Hope," "Death," "Noon"—into something like abstract presences. For these scholars, her punctuation is less an obstacle to meaning than a second grammar operating alongside the words themselves.
ebdbca6c-a13e-45f1-b667-0f0af3ebdc06: Researchers studying stereotype threat have found that people sometimes perform worse on a test when they are reminded of a negative stereotype about a group they belong to. Some critics initially suggested that the women in the first group simply had weaker math skills. However, the participants were assigned to groups at random, and their earlier math grades were similar. Later work by psychologist Toni Schmader and her colleagues pointed to another explanation: worrying about confirming the stereotype seems to use up working memory, the limited mental resource people rely on to keep track of information while solving problems. When that resource is taken up, even well-prepared test takers have less of it left for the task in front of them.
ed5f34b1-7f67-4627-ada9-b98fdc2be1ce: Electrochromic smart windows can shift from clear to tinted when a small voltage is applied. ee0b1b87-30da-44b2-84b7-317b03511c90: For six summers, Werner had left a basket of runner beans on the low fence between his allotment and Sibylle's every Saturday, and every Saturday she had returned it filled with red currants. Werner's beds now produced far more than he could eat, and Sibylle, who had planted her own beans in May, no longer needed his. ______ he kept filling the basket each week, not for the sake of what it held but because setting it on the fence was the only thing he still knew how to say to her.
ee791b4c-0a23-4663-aea0-da7263f5805f: When a metal such as copper is bent or rolled at room temperature, a process called cold working, its internal crystal grains become stretched and crowded with defects. ee88e55f-0f14-4747-a6de-d23904450369: Psychologist Albert Ellis, who developed Rational Emotive Behavior Therapy in the 1950s, argued that emotional disturbance stems less from events themselves than from rigid beliefs about them. eedffc48-47c8-4f08-95be-6c93cac4f4f5: In the cold winter of 1947, Frau Weber spread the parts of her tenant's broken music box across the kitchen table of her Vienna boarding house. ef970c8c-2f80-4624-9d58-cbb447e61b5a: Each evening the tannery vats along the river fell quiet beneath the copper light of the setting sun, and the smell of lime and dye drifted over the water. f02e8d3b-e496-426b-bb5d-f75c53156a2e: Every November, Rodrigo and Estéban met at the shearing shed between their two ranches to see who could clip more ewes before sundown. f15d9a85-a915-4bc2-898c-fbd8e1169b15: During the eighth and ninth centuries, the Byzantine Empire was divided by a bitter dispute over religious images, or icons. Iconoclasts, who sought to remove such images from churches, are often remembered as simple destroyers of art, but historian Leslie Brubaker argues that many of their objections were carefully reasoned. Iconoclast theologians contended that a painted figure of Christ could depict only his human form and not his divine nature, so any such image either separated the two natures or wrongly claimed to capture the divine. Defenders of icons, most notably John of Damascus, responded with an equally technical argument: veneration directed at an image passes to the person it represents, so honoring an icon is not the same as worshipping wood and paint. In Brubaker's view, the controversy was therefore less a clash between lovers and haters of art than a sustained debate about how the divine could, or could not, be made visible.
f2049412-6793-4475-92b0-5db6eefa536c: On the last Friday of the term, Mr. Jayasinghe chalked a single line down the middle of the blackboard while mist drifted over the tea bushes outside the schoolroom window. f2df57f8-5550-4352-acd2-90a4f5a48b59: Some critics have charged that Anselm Kiefer's early works, in which he photographed himself giving the Nazi salute at sites across Europe, risked glamorizing the very regime they invoked. Art historian Lisa Saltzman offers a different reading: she argues that Kiefer staged these gestures not to celebrate the past but to force German viewers of the postwar generation to confront a history their society had largely chosen to leave unspoken. If Saltzman is correct, the works should have provoked discomfort chiefly among audiences who shared that silence, so her interpretation would be most strongly supported if it were found that ______
f3917c64-3215-4c33-9987-d6ca54f4d6c7: In his 1924 Manifesto of Surrealism, André Breton defined automatism as writing or drawing "dictated by thought, in the absence of any control exercised by reason." Because the method excluded deliberate aesthetic choice, Breton argued that its products exposed the workings of the unconscious more faithfully than any carefully planned composition could. ______ he prized even the awkward, unpolished fragments that emerged from automatic sessions, treating their roughness as proof of authenticity rather than as a defect to be corrected.
f39ac689-0631-43fb-846c-e161ada17a6f: When Tsar Alexander II issued the Emancipation Manifesto in 1861, roughly twenty-three million privately owned serfs gained personal freedom: they could marry, own property, and bring cases to court without a landlord's permission. The economic terms of the reform, however, were far less generous. Land was not handed to former serfs outright; instead, peasants received allotments that were often smaller than the plots they had farmed before, and they were required to pay for them through "redemption payments" stretched over forty-nine years. Because these payments were frequently set above the land's market value, many households fell into chronic debt. Moreover, the allotments were usually assigned to the village commune, or mir, rather than to individual families, so peasants could not easily sell their share or leave to seek work elsewhere. Historians therefore argue that although the edict ended the legal bondage of serfdom, it left much of the peasantry tied to the land by financial obligation and communal control for decades afterward.
f49fd449-a1ee-4968-805e-b42ae91f3688: In the short story "Elevator Siding," Pavel Hrynchuk, a retired stationmaster, still lives beside the grain elevator in the Saskatchewan town where he worked for forty-one years. One autumn morning a letter arrives from England containing a faded photograph: a dozen children with name tags pinned to their coats, standing on Pavel's platform in 1940. They were evacuees sent overseas during the war, and Pavel, then a young clerk, had promised one of them, a girl named Margaret, that he would be at the station when her mother came to take her home. The mother never came that winter, and Margaret was eventually placed with a farm family farther west. Some readers see Pavel's decades in the town as simple contentment with prairie life. One critic, however, argues that Pavel never left because he continued to regard himself as bound by his words to Margaret, long after anyone could have held him to them.
f53a9da5-d1b4-4d33-91f4-3c66ffd7811f: In 1966, psychologist Jack Brehm proposed reactance theory to explain a puzzling pattern: people sometimes respond to persuasion by doing the opposite of what they are urged to do. According to Brehm, individuals hold beliefs about which behaviors they are free to choose, and when they perceive that one of those freedoms is being eliminated or threatened, they experience an unpleasant motivational state he called reactance. This state pushes them to restore the threatened freedom, often by valuing the forbidden option more highly or by deliberately performing the discouraged behavior. Later researchers found that the strength of this response depends less on what a message asks for than on how it is framed. In one study, students read identical recommendations to limit their alcohol intake; those who received forceful wording such as "you must" and "any reasonable person would agree" reported stronger intentions to drink than did those who received the same advice phrased as a suggestion.
f584db55-ab78-42e6-b78d-6be980033645: When two different metals are bonded and heated, their atoms migrate across the interface, and they rarely do so at equal rates. In copper–zinc couples, for example, zinc atoms diffuse into copper faster than copper atoms diffuse into zinc, so vacancies pile up on the zinc-rich side and can merge into tiny pores known as Kirkendall voids. Materials engineer Priya Raman treats these voids strictly as defects: in solder joints for electronics, she argues, they concentrate stress and cause cracks, so alloy pairs should be chosen to keep diffusion rates as balanced as possible. Chemist Tomás Ibarra studies the same imbalance for a different purpose. By deliberately heating metal nanoparticles coated with a second element, his team lets the faster-moving core atoms escape outward, leaving behind hollow nanospheres whose large interior surfaces are useful in catalysis. __For Ibarra, then, an unequal diffusion rate is not a mismatch to be engineered away but a parameter to be tuned.__
f6050ed4-e7a7-43ea-afb9-8b4e7ec2a420: In rural Anatolia, carpet weavers working from home have long passed motifs from one generation to the next, treating them as shared village heritage rather than private property. When export firms began registering some of these traditional patterns as their own designs, economist Elif Kaya argued that copyright law, built to reward individual creators, was poorly suited to such crafts. Because a motif may have been refined by hundreds of weavers over centuries, she noted, any attempt to ______ it to a single author is largely arbitrary.
f7238aab-3cb1-4da1-a866-f236af60438a: The American pika, a small relative of the rabbit, lives on rocky alpine slopes in western North America. Because it does not hibernate and carries a dense coat suited to cold, the pika can die after only a few hours of exposure to temperatures around 25°C. Researchers have therefore long predicted that warming summers would push pikas upslope and eliminate low-elevation populations. __Yet surveys in parts of the Columbia River Gorge have found pikas thriving at sites barely above sea level, where summer afternoons regularly exceed that threshold.__ Investigating these sites, ecologist Johanna Varner found that the animals shelter in deep talus and moss-covered rock, where temperatures stay cool, and shift their foraging to early mornings and evenings. Such findings suggest that the pika's vulnerability to warming depends less on air temperature alone than on whether its local terrain offers cool refuges.
f73c3201-d5a4-4807-a9e9-a222f3f39efd: In her research on online communities, Sherry Turkle described multiuser games as possible "identity workshops," spaces where people try out versions of themselves that differ from who they are offline. A research team building on her work surveyed players who keep more than one character, or persona, in online role-playing games. For each player, the team recorded two things: how many personas the player kept and how much those personas differed from the player's offline personality. The team proposes that playing many personas does not by itself lead to self-insight. Instead, the team argues, players gain self-insight when they keep several personas that each differ sharply from their offline selves.
f7d5ee92-1da1-4be1-a25d-f58254b9f212:
The following text is adapted from a short story. Asha, a young girl, is traveling with her grandmother on a houseboat in the backwaters of Kerala, India, a few weeks after her grandfather's death.

At dawn the water was the color of weak tea. Asha woke to find her grandmother already at the edge of the deck, holding a brass bowl of marigold and jasmine petals. Asha had expected her to cry, as she had at the funeral. Instead, her grandmother scattered the petals one handful at a time and watched them drift away with the slow current toward the palms. She did not try to call them back. Asha sat very still beside her. No one had been able to explain to her why the house now felt calm instead of broken, but watching the petals go, she thought she finally understood.
fb0571ea-9508-4390-aa0f-f4df6d8a437e: Supercritical carbon dioxide, a fluid held above 31°C and roughly 73 atmospheres of pressure so that it behaves partly like a gas and partly like a liquid, can seep through tightly packed coffee beans as readily as a vapor ______ it can dissolve caffeine nearly as effectively as the harsh organic solvents it has largely replaced in decaffeination plants.
fb37ca17-8f20-4918-be93-31204f275d66:
When a professor's recommendation letter for a student applying to graduate school in philosophy says only that the student "has excellent handwriting and always attended class," readers rarely conclude that the professor admires the student. Philosopher of language Paul Grice argued that such inferences are not accidents of interpretation but follow from a general expectation that conversation is cooperative: listeners assume that speakers are trying to say as much as is needed, no more, and to be truthful, relevant, and clear. Because the letter conspicuously omits any comment on the student's philosophical ability—the very thing a reader would need to know—the reader infers that the writer has nothing favorable to say about it.

Grice called meanings of this kind "implicatures," and he stressed that they differ from what words literally encode. An implicature can be canceled without contradiction: the professor could add, "and, incidentally, she is the most gifted philosopher I have taught," and the earlier inference would simply dissolve. Literal content cannot be withdrawn this way, which, for Grice, showed that much of what speakers communicate arises from shared assumptions about how conversation works rather than from the words themselves.
fb7c357f-bb72-450b-9739-10af1d0b5477: On July 14, 1789, crowds in Paris stormed the Bastille, a fortress-prison long associated with the king's power to jail people without trial. When the crowd broke in, they found only seven prisoners inside, and none of them was being held for political reasons. Even so, the people of Paris spent the following months taking the building apart stone by stone, and some of its stones were carved into small models of the fortress and sent to towns across France. Because freeing a large number of prisoners clearly was not what made the event important, historians conclude that ______
fb951baf-219b-4a8e-bc0d-4de232ddfc15:
The following text is adapted from a short story set in a market town near Lagos in the 1920s. Mr. Adebayo, who has taught at the schoolhouse for forty years, is giving his last lesson.

The pupils fidgeted, their eyes drifting to the window and the noise of the market traders outside. Mr. Adebayo did not scold them, as he had done every other afternoon. Instead, he wrote a long column of sums on the board, more than the hour could possibly allow, and pressed so hard that the stub of chalk crumbled to almost nothing between his fingers. When a boy in the front row pointed out that nobody could finish so many problems before the bell, the old teacher only nodded and kept writing. The column, it seemed, was not really meant to be solved; rather, by filling the board, Mr. Adebayo was ______
fc02d3b5-a146-4326-bbfc-558b8e7664f6: Composer Pauline Oliveros developed "Deep Listening," a practice in which performers attend not only to sounds they produce but to the entire sonic environment, including breath, room resonance, and distant traffic. Music educator Rachel Mendes argues that Oliveros's exercises belong in conservatory curricula chiefly because they sharpen students' pitch discrimination and ensemble timing—skills already central to conventional training. Musicologist Tomás Ibarra reads Oliveros differently. He notes that her early essays criticized the conservatory model itself, in which a single trained authority decides which sounds count as music and which count as noise. __For Ibarra, the exercises' value lies precisely in dissolving that hierarchy, since a student who learns to treat a cough in the audience as material equal to a scripted chord has stopped deferring to any single arbiter of musical worth.__ Teaching Deep Listening, he concludes, means questioning the institution that would host it.
fc09317a-04d9-43a0-971a-22f1b993b307: In the summer of 1947, British lawyer Cyril Radcliffe was given roughly five weeks to draw the borders dividing British India into India and Pakistan. He had never visited the subcontinent before, worked largely from outdated maps and census figures, and consulted few people with local knowledge. Historians have often focused on these constraints to explain why his lines cut through villages, farmland, and irrigation canals. Yet a number of recent scholars argue that the haste of the drawing explains less about the violence that followed than the decision of how to announce it. Although Radcliffe finished his work before independence on August 15, the final boundaries were withheld until two days afterward. During that gap, millions of people in Punjab and Bengal did not know which country they would live in, and rumors filled the silence. These scholars contend that this uncertainty, more than any particular flaw in where the line ran, allowed local militias to organize and helped turn fear into mass killing and flight.
fe10d4f4-52ec-44bd-9e7c-44c17ad419c4: Historians once attributed the French defeat in Saint-Domingue largely to yellow fever, which killed thousands of soldiers sent by Napoleon in 1802. Recent scholarship, however, emphasizes that the disease's impact was shaped by revolutionary strategy. Toussaint Louverture and his officers understood that newly arrived European troops had no immunity to tropical illnesses, so during the spring campaign they avoided decisive battles, burned coastal towns, and withdrew into the mountainous interior. This approach forced French columns to remain in the lowlands during the rainy season, when mosquito-borne fever spread fastest, while the revolutionary forces preserved their own strength. By the time Jean-Jacques Dessalines led the final offensive in 1803, the French army had been so weakened that it could no longer hold the colony.
